answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
LevelTen Energy is the world's largest clean energy marketplace for corporate and institutional buyers. In the last 10 years, LevelTen has facilitated transactions that supported more than 16 GW of new-build renewable capacity across North America and Europe.

LevelTen is not providing detailed responses to this public consultation for Consequential Methods as we believe that corporate buyers interested in pursuing the standard should have the primary voice. However, we are providing feedback on a specific concern that we feel GHGP should consider, which derives from LevelTen’s unique role at the forefront of storage/hybrid contracting.

With increasing amounts of intermittent renewable energy being deployed each year, battery storage will become critical to achieving grid decarbonization. Batteries will be essential to support time-matched strategies, where buyers need to shift renewable generation to match their load profiles. Batteries will also be crucial to support consequential strategies, allowing buyers to direct charging during low-carbon hours and to discharge during high-emissions hours.

To support both use cases, LevelTen is currently developing process workflows (e.g., EAC/GC
registry interface, charge/discharge record tracking) to deliver a seamless solution that is compliant with all relevant standards. LevelTen’s intent is to then make those “storage shift” solutions available at scale to a range of buyers and sellers, including via bilateral contracting mechanisms and traded products.

Our concern is that consequential accounting methodologies could be drafted in a way that
inadvertently eliminates the opportunity to deliver storage shift at scale, which would undercut a critical tool for corporate decarbonization and storage asset finance. Specifically, we are concerned that a strict application of the “counterfactual” principle inherent in consequential methodologies could prevent corporates from claiming GHG emissions reductions associated with executed storage shift contracts.

As an example, imagine a corporate executes a one-year forward storage shift agreement with an operating storage asset that contractually requires the asset to charge during the lowest emissions hours and discharge during the highest emissions hours each day. Because this contract would dictate the battery’s dispatch over the entire year, we believe the buyer should be able to claim the associated emissions reductions under a consequential methodology.
·
Our concern is that a “strict” counterfactual definition might attempt to remove from the emissions calculation certain days when wholesale market prices suggest the battery “might have” charged and discharged during the same hours dictated by the shift contract. LevelTen would argue strongly that this “strict” interpretation would be technically unreasonable and would, in practice, eliminate a critical storage contracting and dispatch strategy that could deliver meaningful global emissions reductions at scale because:

(a) Even if strict counterfactual analysis suggested that emissions-based dispatch coincided with a hypothetical market-based dispatch, the reality is that the storage shift contract locked in the emissions-based strategy by contractually removing the battery’s operational flexibility.

(b) The strict counterfactual analysis would also assume to know which wholesale market signals (e.g., hourly arbitrage, ancillary services, capacity, etc.) the battery would have followed on a given day when, in fact, that could never be known.

In conclusion, the counterfactual should not be based on some model of how the battery might
have dispatched in the absence of a storage shift contract. Instead, it should be based on the fact that, absent the storage shift contract, the battery would have had total flexibility to pursue whatever strategy it wanted, but the contract removed that flexibility to ensure it would be operated exclusively to lower grid emissions.
